ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Adolescents aged 11-17 with and without MDD were recruited from Washington, D.C. and surrounding areas through social media advertisements, paper advertisements posted in the community, mailings to local zip codes, and community referrals.

> Participants were ineligible for the study if they had an estimated IQ<70; regularly used substances within the previous three months; had ever experienced cardinal bipolar disorder symptoms; met diagnostic criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder, a psychotic disorder, or moderate-to-severe autism spectrum disorder; or had a neurological disorder or unstable medical condition.

> Following data collection, two participants were excluded from analyses because they completed <25% of EMA prompts (a preregistered exclusion criterion ensuring each participant contributed enough observations to reliably estimate within-person effects).

> The sample was 13.85% Hispanic/Latino; 81.54% of participants were neither Hispanic nor Latino, and 4.62% did not report ethnicity.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Mounting evidence suggests that sleep disturbances and depression are linked through disruptions in reward processing.
This pathway may be especially relevant to adolescent depression, as adolescence is characterized by more frequent sleep disturbances, reduced sleep, and refinement of reward circuitry.

Aim: This preregistered study uses high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression Studies (CTADS) cohort (collected from 2023 to 2026) to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia and to determine whether effects exhibit diurnal variation.
Methods: Sixty-five adolescents (12-18 years; 43 female, 22 male; 41 with major depressive disorder, 24 healthy volunteers) completed 120 EMA prompts over 30 days.
Participants reported prior-night sleep disturbances and duration once per day, and anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia four times per day.

We ran two Bayesian multilevel linear models, estimating anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, respectively, as functions of prior-night sleep disturbances, time of day, diagnostic group, and their interactions.
We then ran two exploratory models assessing sleep duration in the same manner.
Results: In adolescents with MDD, whereas self-reported sleep disturbances did not predict anhedonia, longer sleep duration predicted both lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia.
In healthy adolescents, greater sleep disturbances predicted lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia.
Effects of sleep disturbances on anhedonia tended to increase across the day in adolescents with MDD and healthy adolescents.
Conclusions: Sleep disturbances and duration differentially predict next-day anhedonia in adolescents with MDD.
For adolescent MDD patients, treatments that target sleep duration, as opposed to sleep disturbances, could provide more immediate effects on anhedonia.
Time-of- day moderation effects suggest the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.
In adolescents with MDD, whereas self-reported sleep disturbances did not predict anhedonia, longer sleep duration predicted both lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia.
Moderation results suggest that the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

text.text: Second, no studies have examined whether or how effects of sleep on anhedonia might vary by time of day.

Identifying when sleep most strongly influences anhedonia could suggest whether the effects of sleep are driven by circadian rhythms, accumulated sleep pressure, or other timevarying cognitive or affective processes.
Additionally, if associations exhibit diurnal variation, interventions targeting sleep or anhedonia may be more effective when delivered at particular times.

We leveraged data from a high-density EMA study to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia in adolescents with and without MDD, and to determine whether effects exhibit diurnal variation.
We hypothesized that within individuals, sleep disturbances would positively predict anhedonia and that this effect would be stronger in adolescents with MDD compared to healthy adolescents.
We also hypothesized that within individuals, time would moderate the effect of sleep disturbances on anhedonia, such that the effect would weaken across the day.
We expected the moderating effect of time would weaken less across the day in adolescents with MDD compared to healthy adolescents.
In addition to our preregistered analyses pertaining to sleep disturbances, we conducted exploratory analyses pertaining to sleep duration, for which we did not pose a priori hypotheses.

text.text: For each model described below, four Markov chains were run, each with 4,000 iterations.
Package-default, weakly informative priors were used for all fixed effects and variance components.
Sleep disturbances, sleep duration, anticipatory anhedonia, and consummatory anhedonia were person-mean centered prior to analyses.

We ran two Bayesian multilevel linear models (one modeling anticipatory anhedonia and one modeling consummatory anhedonia), with EMA reports (level 1) nested within days (level 2) nested within individuals (level 3).
In each model, anhedonia was estimated as a function of prior-night sleep disturbances (level 2), time of day (level 1), diagnostic group (level 3), and all interactions.
We then re-ran the models including sex (level 3) and age (level 3) as covariates.

All models included random intercepts for participants and for EMA day nested within participants, and random slopes for time, sleep disturbances, and their interaction across participants, with correlations among all participant-level random effects estimated by default.

We ran exploratory analyses investigating the effects of sleep duration on anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, using the same model specifications as in our preregistered analyses, only substituting sleep disturbances with sleep duration.
Inference was based primarily on posterior distributions and 95% credible intervals for model parameters.
We considered posterior probabilities ranging from 0.90 to 0.95 as moderate evidence of effects, and posterior probabilities exceeding 0.95 as strong evidence of effects.

The current study utilized 30 days of EMA data from adolescents with and without MDD to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, and to determine whether effects exhibited diurnal variation.

Self-reported sleep disturbances did not meaningfully impact next-day anhedonia: Sleep disturbances did not predict anticipatory or consummatory anhedonia in adolescents with MDD, and sleep disturbances predicted lower anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia in healthy adolescents.
With respect to sleep duration, however, more sleep predicted lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia specifically in adolescents with MDD.
Time-of-day moderation effects suggest that the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.
Contrary to our hypotheses, sleep disturbances did not predict anticipatory or consummatory anhedonia in adolescents with MDD.
This may reflect a cumulative effect of sleep disturbances on anhedonia that is not observable at the day level.

For example, for an adolescent who usually experiences sleep disturbances, a single night of high-quality sleep may not be sufficient to improve next-day symptoms; instead, symptoms may only be impacted after multiple consecutive nights of sleep.

The notion that symptoms may only improve after an enduring reduction in sleep disturbances is consistent with evidence that adolescents with MDD exhibit greater emotional inertia (their emotional states tend to persist and are difficult to change; e.g., Liu et al., 2026).

text.text: Building on existing literature in healthy adults (Wieman et al., 2022), this is the first study to demonstrate in adolescents with MDD that getting more sleep predicts next-day decreases in both anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia.

text.text: Reduced sleep is associated with diminished effort expenditure in pursuit of rewards, which can result in individuals experiencing less pleasure in the moment and anticipating less future pleasure (Boland et al., 2020; Treadway et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Reduced sleep is associated with diminished effort expenditure in pursuit of rewards, which can result in individuals experiencing less pleasure in the moment and anticipating less future pleasure <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Boland et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Treadway et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep deficits are also known to impair emotion regulation (e.g., Lollies et al., 2022), meaning when adolescents get less sleep, they may have more difficulty upregulating positive affect the next day.

text.text: These alterations may occur because sleep duration constrains the time available for nocturnal processes implicated in depression.
For example, reduced sleep limits the opportunity for synaptic homeostasis within reward and affective regions, which may contribute to the pathophysiology of depression (Wang et al., 2025b).
text.formatted: For example, reduced sleep limits the opportunity for synaptic homeostasis within reward and affective regions, which may contribute to the pathophysiology of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Wang et al., 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, not getting enough sleep can disrupt the consolidation of emotional memory (Niu et al., 2025; Bennion et al., 2015; Hutchison & Rathore, 2015), impairing individuals' ability to accurately valuate (and, in turn, seek out) potential future rewards based on past pleasurable experiences.

text.text: Contrarily, in healthy adolescents, self-reported sleep duration was not associated with next-day anhedonia.
This may be because healthy adolescents lack the underlying vulnerabilities associated with MDD.
MDD is characterized by altered reward processing and dysregulation in frontolimbic circuitry involved in emotion regulation (e.g., Miller et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: MDD is characterized by altered reward processing and dysregulation in frontolimbic circuitry involved in emotion regulation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Miller et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For adolescents with MDD, reduced sleep may further compromise these systems (by limiting the time available for nocturnal process, as described above), leading to increases in anhedonia; however, for healthy adolescents without these pre-existing aberrations, the effects of reduced sleep on these systems may not be pronounced enough to impact anhedonia the following day.

Findings concerning the moderating effects of time of day suggest that the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

The associations between sleep disturbances and consummatory anhedonia increased across the day in adolescents with MDD and healthy adolescents, and the same was found for anticipatory anhedonia in healthy adolescents.
The fact that sleep disturbances were more positively associated with anhedonia later in the day suggests that accumulated sleep pressure, fatigue, or related circadian processes may be implicated.

Conversely, time did not moderate the effects of sleep duration in either group, supporting the notion that the effects of sleep duration may be related to nocturnal processes, such as synaptic homeostasis or consolidation of emotional memory, as opposed to diurnal biological processes.
Several considerations should be made when interpreting the present findings and identifying directions for future research.
First, the current study only employs subjective measures of sleep; future work should integrate subjective and objective measures to facilitate a broader investigation of sleep effects.
Second, while the current study examines whether sleep variables predict anhedonia, these effects are likely bidirectional.
Putative bidirectional processes should be examined in future work using methods like dynamic structural equation modeling, which are well-suited to bidirectional and autoregressive frameworks.
Additionally, in the current sample, healthy adolescents reported a relatively low incidence of sleep disturbances (see Table S1), which may have introduced floor effects.

text.text: To better understand whether findings are unique to adolescents with MDD, future researchers may wish to include a sample of adolescents with significant sleep disturbances who are otherwise healthy.
More female than male adolescents enrolled in the study, consistent with the higher prevalence rate of MDD in adolescent females relative to males (Brody & Hughes, 2025).

text.text: The racial composition of the current sample was broadly representative of the U.S. population.

While this enhances the generalizability of findings to the broad population, findings may not generalize to racial groups that are underrepresented nationally, such as American Indians and Alaskan Natives.

To our knowledge, the present study is one of only a few to examine person-specific, within-day effects of sleep on anhedonia, and is the first to examine these effects specifically in adolescents with MDD.
We found that more sleep consistently predicted lower anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia in adolescents with MDD.
In contrast, sleep disturbances were not meaningfully associated with next-day anhedonia.
Thus, for adolescent MDD patients, treatments that target sleep duration, as opposed to sleep disturbances, could provide more immediate effects on anhedonia.

Notably, associations between sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) and anhedonia varied across the day, suggesting that the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

More broadly, these findings provide a potentially fruitful direction for future research on adolescent depression and anhedonia, particularly research incorporating complementary, objective sleep measures.
